ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns, with informal pre-meeting chatter made up of short, fragmented exchanges and the formal presentations delivered as extended, slide-guided monologues. Overlap and interruptions are low but present in the casual opening and question periods, where speakers occasionally jump in with brief acknowledgments or self-corrections. The tone is collegial, relaxed, and professionally informal: participants use frequent fillers (“um,” “yeah,” “okay”), repetitions, false starts, and lightly ungrammatical or compressed phrasing, especially among nonnative speakers. Questions are often prefaced with praise, disclaimers such as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” question, and several hedges before reaching the point. Speakers build on prior remarks by restating part of the answer, connecting it to their own work, or proposing follow-up ideas; challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity or uncertainty rather than opposition. Responses are expansive, exploratory, and willing to admit limits, often ending with open questions or future directions.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.

Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Building a wrist-worn sensor and model that flags irregular heart rhythm early enough for a clinic to follow up.

speakers.name: Priya Nandakumar
speakers.background: A fourth-year computer science PhD student working on time-series machine learning for wearable health data. She has built prototype classifiers for arrhythmia screening from photoplethysmography and inertial-sensor streams, using supervised learning, calibration analysis, cross-validation, and error audits. Her current model was trained on a limited set of labeled recordings and has not yet been tested on representative outpatient use data.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya treats the device as a measurement-and-generalization problem: the classifier can only be trusted to the extent that its training labels, signal conditions, and evaluation population resemble real use. She emphasizes separating poor signal quality from rhythm predictions, estimating false-positive behavior rather than reporting only aggregate accuracy, monitoring for model drift, and determining whether inference can run within on-device compute and battery limits.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Mateo Alvarez
speakers.background: A biomedical engineer with 12 years of experience developing optical biosensors and wearable physiological-monitoring prototypes. His work includes photoplethysmography hardware, accelerometer-based motion-artifact characterization, benchtop optical testing, ergonomic wrist-placement studies, and power-budget measurements. He has compared two prototype wrist placements and found substantial movement-related degradation in optical pulse signals.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Mateo sees the model's performance as downstream of a physical sensing chain that must be characterized before the hardware design is fixed. He presses the group to learn how fit, skin contact, placement, ordinary arm motion, ambient light, and battery-management choices affect usable signal. He is wary of treating algorithmic filtering as a substitute for understanding artifact sources, while recognizing that the initial outpatient study should show whether the sensor can collect interpretable data during normal movement.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Lauren Okafor
speakers.background: A cardiology postdoctoral researcher and practicing physician with 7 years of clinical training, focused on ambulatory rhythm monitoring and care pathways for suspected atrial fibrillation and other intermittent arrhythmias. She has worked with Holter monitors, patch monitors, ECG interpretation, chart review, and outpatient triage processes, and has studied how screening alerts affect patient anxiety, clinic workload, and downstream testing.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Lauren frames an alert as a clinical communication that must lead to a defensible next step, not as a diagnosis. She prioritizes comparison with an appropriate clinical reference assessment, clarity about who reviews alerts and how confirmation occurs, and avoiding escalation to urgent care for low-confidence device findings alone. She supports a small prospective outpatient feasibility study centered on usable signals and calibrated alerts, while noting that regulatory planning will eventually be necessary once the intended-use and follow-up claims become more defined.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a research meeting among a computer scientist, a biomedical engineer, and a cardiologist. The participants should converge on a clear initial direction: a small prospective outpatient feasibility study of the wrist device, with the main aims of measuring signal quality during ordinary movement and estimating alert performance against a clinical reference assessment. The biomedical engineer should explain that wrist placement and motion artifact need to be characterized before locking hardware. The computer scientist should state that the current model needs representative labeled data, that false-positive rate and model drift will matter, and that on-device compute and battery constraints should be measured. The cardiologist should state that alerts require a defined reviewer and confirmation process, and that low-confidence alerts should not automatically trigger urgent care. They should acknowledge that regulatory planning will eventually be needed. Keep the discussion collaborative and technically grounded. Do not have the group create a complete action plan: leave owners, deadlines, study protocol details, reference-assessment logistics, data-governance details, success thresholds, and a finalized alert-review workflow unassigned or only generally noted.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: Hi—sorry, I missed the last meeting, so could I get the quick version of where we landed on the wrist placement and the classifier? For today, I'd like us to get concrete about what an alert actually means in the outpatient study, what information comes with it, who sees it, and what confirmation we can realistically offer without treating every low-confidence notification like an urgent event, because...

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: On placement, both sites gave us a usable pulse when people were still, but normal arm movement degraded both, and the one with the stronger average signal wasn't consistently cleaner during movement. So I'd be careful about defining an alert until we know whether the optical segment was actually, um, interpretable. Otherwise we may be routing fit or motion problems into Lauren's follow-up pathway.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: That separation is essential for the classifier too. Right now, it can produce a fairly confident rhythm score on a weak, low-motion pulse segment, so I wouldn't let the score itself stand in for interpretability. We need a quality state first, and then an alert only for interpretable windows. Mateo, do you have a sense of which quality indicators stay reliable across the two placements during ordinary movement?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Not yet, honestly. The simple optical amplitude measures help when someone is still, but with repeated arm motion they can still look okay while the pulse shape gets distorted. The accelerometer helps, but it doesn't catch loose contact or a little ambient-light leak. I'd want to look at pulse-shape consistency, contact-related indicators, and motion all together, separately for each placement, before we claim a quality gate transfers to normal use.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: That makes sense. For the study, I think we should keep those component measures separate instead of collapsing them right away into one gate, because otherwise we can't tell whether a missed or false alert came from contact, motion, or the rhythm model. I've also seen a few clean-looking traces get rejected already, so I'd want to inspect that before we fix thresholds.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: Keep them separate. Clinically, if a trace was clean enough to interpret but the gate suppressed it, that is a different failure from a noisy segment generating an alert, and we need both visible when we compare against the reference monitor. Priya, what are the false positives you’ve looked at so far? Are they mostly motion-related, or do they look like regular rhythms with enough beat-to-beat variation to, um, fool the model?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: I've only looked at them in cross-validation, so I wouldn't over-interpret the pattern. Some are clearly weak-amplitude segments despite low accelerometer motion, but others look more like regular rhythms with variable pulse intervals. I can't yet tell whether that's true physiological variability, preprocessing, or the small, small training set. For the outpatient study, I think we need the reference labels tied to the alert windows so we can separate those cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: And that window-level linkage is non-negotiable for me. Otherwise we end up calling something a device false positive when the reference was sampled at a different time. The practical question is what reference we can put on these outpatients that they'll actually wear, and whether the clinic can review enough of it to adjudicate alerts. I need to check what capacity we have before pretending a continuous reference is automatic.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That linkage matters for the hardware readout too. If the reference is intermittent instead of continuous, could we at least time-stamp the quality components and keep a short raw optical segment around every alert, and maybe around quality rejections too? Otherwise, if an alert has no matching reference window, we won't know if it was rhythm uncertainty or just the wrist signal falling apart.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: I think that is worth preserving, especially the rejected windows. From the modeling side, I would want the raw segment, the timestamps, the separate quality components, and the model score, not just the final alert, so we can audit whether a failure is the gate or the classifier. The storage cost may matter on the prototype, though. Mateo, do we know roughly how much buffered raw data we can retain?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Not from the benchtop numbers, no. We have enough memory for short event clips, but I need to check the actual battery and storage cost on the intended device. Especially if we keep rejected windows too, because the higher optical duty cycle and accelerometer processing may be the limiting part. I'd rather- I'd define a modest pre- and post-buffer around the alert or rejection than assume we can log continuously.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: I think modest clips are probably enough for feasibility, as long as we're deliberate about which ones. For the clinical comparison, every alert needs its time-stamped segment, but a sampled set of rejected windows, especially ones that look, look clean by the other measures, may be more useful than saving every bad-quality period. Otherwise the review burden gets silly pretty fast.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I'd support sampling the rejections rather than trying to retain every one. But I'd make sure the sample is stratified, low-motion, apparently good-contact rejections, as well as obvious motion and loose-fit cases, because the deceptively clean-looking failures are the ones the simple quality measures may miss. I need to see what that does to the on-device power budget before we pick the clip length.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: And from the clinic side, the sampling scheme should protect us from fooling ourselves about a reassuring gate. If we only retain the obvious failures, we’ll never see the clean-appearing rejected windows that may, may contain something clinically relevant. Mateo, when you check the power budget, could you include what it would take to keep a random background sample too, not just event-triggered clips?

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I can include that comparison. I need to separate the cost of retaining the clips from the cost of collecting at the optical rate we need in the first place, because the background sample may be cheap to store, but if it makes us keep the sensor awake differently, that's not cheap. And for the random sample, do we want it across ordinary wear time, or- are we talking specifically about the periods the device itself calls low quality?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: Across ordinary wear time, I think, plus an intentional oversample of device-labeled low-quality periods. We need some denominator for how often the gate is excluding data in real life, not just a museum of failures. But the low-quality stratum is where we can see whether it’s actually, actually protecting us from misleading alerts. The exact ratio can follow whatever the battery budget tolerates.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: That seems like the right split. One thing I'd like to avoid, though, is treating device-labeled low quality as a single thing in the sampling. We should retain the component flags with each clip, so later we can tell ordinary arm motion from contact loss or light leak. I'll check what random background plus that oversample costs at a few, a few clip lengths. I don't know yet whether the optical duty cycle, rather than storage, is the real constraint.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: Mm, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly. And for the clinic, I’d want the quality state visible alongside any alert, not necessarily every component in the patient-facing message, but enough for the reviewer to know whether it’s a reasonably interpretable rhythm finding or a very, uh, qualified one. We can keep the actual wording and who receives it provisional until I check what reference-monitoring and review capacity we can support.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: Right, okay.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: One small modeling constraint while those checks are happening. We shouldn't finalize the alert threshold from the existing cross-validation. The outpatient distribution is probably different enough that we need to treat this as a feasibility calibration exercise, and report false-positive rates and usable-signal rates by placement and quality stratum. I also need to verify that the preprocessing and inference actually fit the prototype's compute and battery budget, not just my development setup.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: And I’d add that placement can’t just be a covariate in that report. The stronger resting pulse site wasn’t reliably the less, um, corrupted one during movement, so usable-signal and false-alert rates really do need to stay separated by placement until we have outpatient data. Otherwise we may lock the hardware around the wrong bench result.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: For the feasibility study, I’d keep placement separate all the way through the clinical readout too. If one site produces more qualified alerts but fewer interpretable windows, that’s not something we can just average away. I’ll check the realistic reference-monitor options and reviewer capacity, and then we can decide what alert review actually- what that looks like, rather than implying this is ready for patient-facing notification.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Alvarez
transcript.text: I think that covers what we needed today. I’ll bring the power numbers back once I’ve checked them. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lauren Okafor
transcript.text: Sounds good. Take care, both.
